newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. enlisted soldier denies sex charges.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. enlisted soldier denies sex charges.

text.p: The U.S. Army's top enlisted soldier on Wednesday denied all charges filed against him in a sexual misconduct case that has rocked the American military.

"I am not answering to any of these charges because I have not done anything that I've been charged with," Army Sgt. Major Gene McKinney said in a statement to reporters outside his lawyer's office in Alexandria, Virginia, a Washington suburb.

"I want the American people to know, and I certainly want the American soldier ... to know, that I have done no wrong in these charges," said McKinney, a 22-year veteran and the only soldier who carries the U.S. military title sergeant-major of the Army. His wife, Wilhemina, stood by his side.

The Army announced earlier on Wednesday that it had appointed a senior officer to investigate whether there was sufficient evidence to court-martial McKinney on 18 sexual misconduct charges lodged against him by three Army women and a female sailor. They claim he made improper sexual advances toward them or committed other misconduct, including adultery, over a three-year period.

McKinney, 46, was suspended in February from his Pentagon job as the senior enlisted adviser to service leaders pending resolution of the allegations. His was the latest and highest-profile chapter in a sexual harassment scandal that has shaken the Army and resulted Tuesday in the sentencing of another sergeant to 25 years in prison for rape.

McKinney's lawyer, Charles Gittins, was asked if he felt his client, who is black, was the victim of racial prejudice. Gittins replied: "I'm not sure if there's a race issue. I know that in every interview, CID (Army investigators) asked witnesses whether Sgt. Major McKinney was only interested in white women. If there's a race issue it's been injected by the investigators and that's of great concern to me."
